lesson.title: Bribery, Insult, and the Diplomatic Crisis That Nearly Meant War
lesson.summary: When French agents demanded bribes from American envoys in 1797 before agreeing to negotiate, the resulting XYZ Affair outraged the American public and pushed John Adams's presidency toward an undeclared war with France.
lesson.body:
By 1797, relations between the United States and France had deteriorated badly. France viewed the Jay Treaty, which the United States had signed with Britain in 1794, as a betrayal of the alliance the two countries had formed during the American Revolution, and French warships and privateers began seizing American merchant vessels trading with Britain. Hoping to avoid war, President John Adams sent a three man commission, Charles Cotesworth Pinckney, John Marshall, and Elbridge Gerry, to Paris in 1797 to negotiate a settlement and restore normal relations.

When the American envoys arrived, they were not received by France's foreign minister, Charles Maurice de Talleyrand, but instead approached by intermediaries who demanded a substantial bribe for Talleyrand personally and a loan to the French government before any formal negotiations could even begin. The Americans refused these demands and, after months of fruitless waiting, most of the commission returned home without ever formally meeting French officials.

When Adams reported the affair to Congress, he withheld the names of the French agents, referring to them only as X, Y, and Z, a label that gave the episode its lasting name. The published dispatches, once released to the public, caused outrage across the country. Many Americans who had previously sympathized with revolutionary France, a legacy of the alliance dating back to the Revolutionary War and reinforced by Jefferson's own pro-French leanings during his time as Secretary of State, felt betrayed by what looked like an attempt to humiliate and extort the United States.

A popular slogan, often summarized as millions for defense but not one cent for tribute, captured the public mood, though its exact origin is debated among historians rather than being a verified statement by any single envoy. The scandal produced a surge of nationalist sentiment and support for Adams and the Federalists, who used the crisis to expand the navy, strengthen the army, and push through the Alien and Sedition Acts, arguing that French sympathizers and immigrants posed a genuine internal security threat. Congress created a separate Department of the Navy in 1798 and authorized new warships, while towns across the country held rallies and sent Adams letters pledging support against French aggression, a striking reversal from the pro-French enthusiasm many Americans had shown earlier in the decade.

The XYZ Affair pushed the United States into the Quasi War, an undeclared naval conflict with France that lasted from 1798 to 1800, testing Adams's presidency at nearly every turn. Adams resisted the loudest Federalist calls for a full declaration of war and eventually sent a new peace commission that ended the conflict through the Convention of 1800, but not before the affair had reshaped domestic politics, fueling the very party passions Washington had warned against in his Farewell Address and setting the stage for the repressive legislation that would define the final years of Adams's term.
